kurals.tamil:
தள்ளா விளையுளும் தக்காரும் தாழ்விலாச்
செல்வரும் சேர்வது நாடு.
kurals.transliteration:
Thallaa vilaiyulum thakkaarum thaazhvilaach
chelvarum servadhu naadu.
kurals.meaning: A true country is one where three things come together: harvests that never fail, people of real worth, and wealthy citizens whose riches do not decline.
kurals.elementary: Think of a good neighbourhood. The gardens always grow food, there are wise grown-ups you can ask for help, and the shopkeepers do well enough to keep their shops open. When all three are there together, it feels like a real home. Valluvar says a country is the same.
kurals.university: The chapter opens the Kural’s treatment of naadu (the realm or territory), the third of the six angas (limbs) of kingship listed in kural 381, and it begins with a definition by constituents. Thallaa vilaiyul is literally ‘produce that does not fail’ (thal, to reject or fall off), thakkaar are ‘the worthy’, whom Parimelazhagar glosses as men of virtue and learning, and thaazhvilaa chelvar are ‘the wealthy without decline’, whom he identifies as merchants whose stock never runs out; Pope’s prose gloss follows him in naming merchants. Modern commentators widen the reading: Solomon Pappaiah turns the first term into the labourers who produce the harvest and the third into the unselfish rich, while Kalaignar reads the wealthy as those who do not squander riches on evil ends. The verb servadhu (that in which they gather together) makes the point that a land is defined by the coexistence of these groups, not by any one of them. The sandhi-joined text reads ‘விளையுளுந் தக்காருந்’ and ‘செல்வருஞ்’, which divide into the same words.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Valmiki’s opening description of Ayodhya under King Dasaratha paints a city whose people were learned, virtuous and content with their own wealth, where no one was poor, miserly or uneducated, and whose granaries and treasuries were full.
hinduism.explanation: The Ramayana begins its story by showing the ideal kingdom: a place that is rich in goods and also rich in good and learned people.
hinduism.tie_back: Ayodhya brings together the same three things as the Kural: plenty, worthy people and wealth that does not run out.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda, Sarga 6 (description of Ayodhya)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close thematic match. Valmiki describes the ideal city in far more detail, and the Kural’s precise three-part definition is its own.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Charge them that are rich in this world, that they be not highminded, nor trust in uncertain riches, but in the living God, who giveth us richly all things to enjoy; That they do good, that they be rich in good works, ready to distribute, willing to communicate.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells Timothy to teach wealthy believers not to be proud or rely on riches, but to use them generously for others.
christianity.tie_back: Modern commentators read the Kural’s ‘wealthy without decline’ as the rich who spend well, which is exactly Paul’s ideal of the rich.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches only one of the Kural’s three elements (the right kind of wealthy person). Paul says nothing about harvests or the definition of a country.

islam.quote_or_event: “There was for [the tribe of] Saba’ in their dwelling place a sign: two [fields of] gardens on the right and on the left. [They were told], ‘Eat from the provisions of your Lord and be grateful to Him. A good land [have you], and a forgiving Lord.’”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an recalls the people of Sheba, who lived between two great gardens and were told they had been given a good land.
islam.tie_back: Saba’s gardens on either side are a picture of the Kural’s unfailing harvest, the first mark of a real country.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong on abundance and ‘a good land’. The Qur’an stresses gratitude to God, while the Kural adds worthy people and merchants.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For the LORD thy God bringeth thee into a good land, a land of brooks of water, of fountains and depths that spring out of valleys and hills; A land of wheat, and barley, and vines, and fig trees, and pomegranates; a land of oil olive, and honey; A land wherein thou shalt eat bread without scarceness, thou shalt not lack any thing in it.”
judaism.explanation: Moses describes the promised land to Israel as a place of water, grain and fruit where bread will never be scarce.
judaism.tie_back: ‘Bread without scarceness’ is the Torah’s version of the Kural’s ‘harvest that never fails’.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close on the unfailing harvest. Deuteronomy does not mention the worthy people or the wealthy class the Kural adds.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Cakkavatti Sihanada Sutta, the Buddha foretells a future age when India will be rich and prosperous, its villages, towns and royal cities so close together that a cockerel could fly from one to the next, under a righteous wheel-turning king.
buddhism.explanation: After a long decline, people return to good conduct and the land becomes crowded, fertile and wealthy again.
buddhism.tie_back: The Buddhist ideal realm, like the Kural’s, is a land where plenty and good people exist together.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good fit for the picture of an ideal prosperous realm, though the sutta links prosperity to moral renewal rather than listing its parts.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “The fruits never rot nor fail all the year round, neither winter nor summer, for the air is so soft that a new crop ripens before the old has dropped.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus reaches the land of the Phaeacians and sees King Alcinous’ orchard, where pears, apples, figs and grapes are always in season.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Homer’s orchard where fruit ‘never fails’ is the mythic picture of the Kural’s thallaa vilaiyul, the harvest that never fails.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Near-exact image for the first element of the Kural. It describes a royal garden rather than a whole country.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “First, there must be food; secondly, arts, for life requires many instruments; thirdly, there must be arms ... fourthly, there must be a certain amount of revenue, both for internal needs, and for the purposes of war.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle lists the functions a city cannot do without, starting with food and going on to crafts, arms, revenue, worship and justice.
philosophy.tie_back: Like Valluvar, Aristotle defines a state by the things and people it must contain, and food comes first on both lists.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Same method of defining a polity by its essential parts. Aristotle’s list is longer and includes arms and religion.

kurals.tamil:
பெரும்பொருளால் பெட்டக்க தாகி அருங்கேட்டால்
ஆற்ற விளைவது நாடு.
kurals.transliteration:
Perumporulaal pettakka thaaki arungettaal
aatra vilaivadhu naadu.
kurals.meaning: A true country is so rich that others desire it, is free from ruinous calamities, and yields a very large harvest.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a garden so lovely and full of fruit that everyone in town wishes it were theirs. It is not flooded or eaten by pests, and every year it gives more than enough. That is what a good country is like.
kurals.university: Perumporul is ‘great wealth’, and pettakkadhu means ‘that which is desirable’; Parimelazhagar takes the desire to be that of other kingdoms, so the kural admits that a rich land will be coveted, which prepares for the next chapter on fortification (Aran). Arungettaal is read by Parimelazhagar as arum-kedu, ‘with destructive causes being absent’ (arumai here meaning scarcity or absence), and Solomon Pappaiah lists the traditional calamities meant: excessive rain, drought, wild beasts, harmful birds and misrule. Aatra vilaivadhu means ‘yielding abundantly’. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read pettakkadhu more generally as ‘praised and desired by all’. The sandhi-joined text runs the words together as ‘பெட்டக்க தாகி யருங்கேட்டா லாற்ற’, with no change in meaning.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Let him settle in a country which is open and has a dry climate, where grain is abundant, which is chiefly (inhabited) by Aryans, not subject to epidemic diseases (or similar troubles), and pleasant, where the vassals are obedient and his own (people easily) find their livelihood.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu tells the king what kind of country to make his home: one with plenty of grain, free from disease and other troubles, and pleasant to live in.
hinduism.tie_back: Manu’s abundant, pleasant and trouble-free country matches the Kural’s desirable, calamity-free land of great yield.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close in its list of what makes a territory desirable. Manu’s verse also includes ethnic and political criteria that the Kural does not share.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And Lot lifted up his eyes, and beheld all the plain of Jordan, that it was well watered every where, before the LORD destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah, even as the garden of the LORD.”
christianity.explanation: When Abraham and Lot must separate, Lot looks at the fertile Jordan plain and chooses it because it is so rich and well watered.
christianity.tie_back: The plain is the kind of land the Kural describes: so rich that others want it for themselves.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good image of a land desired for its richness. The same verse warns of its coming destruction, which runs against the Kural’s ‘free from calamity’.

islam.quote_or_event: “And if only the people of the cities had believed and feared Allah, We would have opened upon them blessings from the heaven and the earth; but they denied [the messengers], so We seized them for what they were earning.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says abundance from sky and earth would have come to towns that were faithful, while calamity came to those that were not.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s land of great yield and no calamity is, in Qur’anic terms, a land on which blessings have been opened.
islam._accuracy_note: Matches the pairing of abundance and freedom from disaster. The Qur’an makes both depend on faith, which the Kural does not say.

judaism.quote_or_event: “We came unto the land whither thou sentest us, and surely it floweth with milk and honey; and this is the fruit of it.”
judaism.explanation: The spies Moses sent into Canaan come back with huge clusters of fruit and report that the land is wonderfully rich.
judaism.tie_back: Canaan is desired because of its fruit, which is what the Kural means by a land made desirable by its great wealth.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong on desirability through abundance. The spies go on to report that the land is strongly defended, which is a different emphasis.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Mahasudassana Sutta the Buddha describes Kusavati, the royal city of an ancient righteous king, as rich, prosperous, crowded with people and well supplied with food, and never silent with the sounds of festivity.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells Ananda that the small town where he is dying was once this splendid capital, and then teaches that all such splendour passes.
buddhism.tie_back: Kusavati is the Buddhist picture of the desirable land the Kural praises, full of wealth and food.
buddhism._accuracy_note: The prosperity is described in detail, but the sutta’s aim is to show that it does not last, which is the reverse of the Kural’s aim.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “If they had had these they would have colonized the island, for it is a very good one, and would yield everything in due season.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus describes a fertile island near the Cyclopes with meadows, deep soil and a safe harbour, which nobody works because the Cyclopes have no ships.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Homer’s island is the kind of land others would covet for its yield, which is how Parimelazhagar reads the Kural’s ‘desirable’.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good fit for the idea of a land that invites others to want it. The island is empty and uncultivated, so it lacks the rest of the Kural’s picture.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Republic, Socrates says that once a city wants luxuries beyond its needs, its land will no longer be enough, so it will have to cut off a slice of its neighbours’ land, and the neighbours will want a slice of its land too. That, he says, is the origin of war.
philosophy.explanation: Plato traces war back to one land coveting another land’s wealth.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the danger hidden in the Kural’s word ‘desirable’: a rich land draws envy, which is why the next chapter turns to fortresses.
philosophy._accuracy_note: An indirect match. Plato explains why rich lands are coveted, while the Kural simply treats being coveted as a sign of wealth.

kurals.tamil:
பொறையொருங்கு மேல்வருங்கால் தாங்கி இறைவற்கு
இறையொருங்கு நேர்வது நாடு.
kurals.transliteration:
Poraiyorungu melvarungaal thaangi iraivarku
iraiyorungu nervadhu naadu.
kurals.meaning: A true country can carry a heavy load when it suddenly falls on it all at once, and still pay its ruler his full dues.
kurals.elementary: Picture a strong family. When cousins suddenly arrive because their house was flooded, the family makes room and shares its food, and it still pays its bills on time. A good country is strong in the same way.
kurals.university: Porai is ‘burden’ and orungu ‘all together’, so the first line describes a load that arrives all at once. Parimelazhagar specifies the load as people fleeing from neighbouring lands in distress, and Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah follow him, Pappaiah adding refugees from war and natural disaster. The second line plays on the double sense of irai: iraivan is the king and irai is the tax due to him, so a land ‘yields fully the king’s due to the king’ (iraivarku irai orungu nervadhu). The kural therefore measures a country’s strength by its surplus, since only a land with reserves can absorb strangers and still pay its revenue gladly. The sandhi text reads ‘மேல்வருங்காற் றாங்கி யிறைவற் கிறையொருங்கு’, the same words joined.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “As the leech, the calf, and the bee take their food little by little, even so must the king draw from his realm moderate annual taxes.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu tells the king to take taxes gently, a little at a time, so that the country is never drained.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s land pays its full dues willingly, and Manu explains the other half of that bargain: the king must tax lightly.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Matches the tax element only, and from the king’s side rather than the land’s. The burden of incoming people is not addressed.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For for this cause pay ye tribute also: for they are God’s ministers, attending continually upon this very thing. Render therefore to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due; custom to whom custom.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells the Christians in Rome to pay taxes and customs to the authorities as a duty.
christianity.tie_back: Paul’s ‘render to all their dues’ is the attitude of the Kural’s land, which gives the king his due in full.
christianity._accuracy_note: Clear match on paying dues to rulers. Paul does not speak of a land’s capacity to carry sudden burdens.

islam.quote_or_event: “And [also for] those who were settled in al-Madinah and [adopted] the faith before them. They love those who emigrated to them and find not any want in their breasts of what the emigrants were given but give [them] preference over themselves, even though they are in privation.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an praises the Ansar of Medina, who welcomed the emigrants from Mecca and shared with them even when they themselves were in need.
islam.tie_back: Medina carrying the load of the emigrants is exactly the burden Parimelazhagar sees in this kural: newcomers arriving all at once.
islam._accuracy_note: Very close to Parimelazhagar’s reading of the burden as incoming people. The Qur’an praises self-sacrifice, while the Kural praises a land rich enough to cope.

judaism.quote_or_event: Under Solomon, the Book of Kings says, Judah and Israel were as many as the sand of the sea, eating, drinking and rejoicing; twelve district officers each supplied the king’s household for one month of the year, and the people dwelt safely, every man under his vine and fig tree.
judaism.explanation: Solomon’s kingdom is shown as so prosperous that it fed a very large population and also kept the royal court supplied.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s strong land: it carries a great population and still meets the king’s dues in full.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good fit for a land that supports both people and king. Later chapters show Solomon’s taxes as oppressive, which complicates the picture.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Kutadanta Sutta the Buddha tells of a king whose land is plagued by bandits. His wise chaplain advises him not to raise taxes or punish, but to give seed and fodder to farmers, capital to traders and proper wages to officials. The people prosper, crime ends, and the king’s revenue grows.
buddhism.explanation: The story teaches that a prosperous people is what makes a ruler’s revenue secure, not heavier taxes.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s land pays the king in full because it has surplus; the Kutadanta story shows how that surplus is created.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close on the link between a thriving land and full royal revenue. The sutta speaks to the king, while the Kural praises the land.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “We will recoup ourselves by the levy of a general rate; for private individuals cannot be expected to bear the burden of such a handsome present.”
greek_mythology.explanation: King Alcinous of the Phaeacians has his nobles give rich gifts to the stranger Odysseus and says the cost will be met by a levy on the whole people.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Phaeacian land shoulders the cost of a stranger and meets it through a common levy, much as the Kural’s land bears a sudden burden and pays its dues.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Interesting parallel of a people sharing the cost of a stranger, but it concerns one guest, not a mass of newcomers.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Productive of subsistence not only to its own people, but also to outsiders on occasions of calamities ... capable of bearing the burden of a vast army and heavy taxation ... these are the qualities of a good country.”
philosophy.explanation: Kautilya lists the marks of a good country (janapada), including feeding outsiders in times of calamity and bearing heavy taxation.
philosophy.tie_back: Kautilya names both halves of this kural: supporting outsiders in their distress and carrying the burden of the king’s taxes.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Almost point for point the same idea, and likely from a shared Indian tradition of statecraft.

kurals.tamil:
உறுபசியும் ஓவாப் பிணியும் செறுபகையும்
சேரா தியல்வது நாடு.
kurals.transliteration:
Urupasiyum ovaap piniyum serupakaiyum
seraa thiyalvadhu naadu.
kurals.meaning: A true country runs its course untouched by crushing hunger, endless disease and destructive enemies.
kurals.elementary: A happy home is one where nobody goes to bed hungry, nobody is sick all the time, and nobody is afraid of bullies breaking in. Valluvar says a good country is a whole land like that.
kurals.university: The kural names the classic triad of public calamity: urupasi (severe hunger, famine), ovaap pini (disease that does not cease, that is, epidemic) and serupakai (enemies who destroy). Parimelazhagar notes that the third means enemies who come from outside and attack, since internal enmity is treated separately in the next kural. The verb iyalvadhu (that which goes on, continues) suggests a lasting condition rather than a single lucky year. The same trio of famine, pestilence and war recurs in Sanskrit, biblical and Greek accounts of disaster, which makes this one of the most widely shared ideas in the chapter. The sandhi text reads ‘உறுபசியு மோவாப் பிணியுஞ் செறுபகையுஞ்’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: At the close of the Yuddha Kanda, Valmiki describes Rama’s reign: no widows mourned, there was no fear of wild beasts or disease, no robbers, the rains came in season, trees were always in fruit, and people lived long lives free from sickness.
hinduism.explanation: This description of Rama Rajya became the classic Indian picture of a perfect realm.
hinduism.tie_back: Rama Rajya is a land with no hunger, no sickness and no danger, the three absences the Kural makes the test of a country.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda, Sarga 128 (Rama’s reign)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong match on freedom from famine, disease and fear. Valmiki attributes it to Rama’s righteousness rather than to the land itself.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Nation shall rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom: And great earthquakes shall be in divers places, and famines, and pestilences.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns his disciples of the calamities to come: war, earthquake, famine and plague.
christianity.tie_back: Luke lists the very evils the Kural’s good country is free from: enemies, famine and pestilence.
christianity._accuracy_note: The same triad of evils, but described as signs of the end rather than as the absence that marks a good land.

islam.quote_or_event: “Let them worship the Lord of this House, Who has fed them, [saving them] from hunger and made them safe, [saving them] from fear.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an reminds the Quraysh of Mecca that God protected their city from hunger and from fear.
islam.tie_back: Freedom from hunger and from the fear of enemies are two of the Kural’s three marks of a good land.
islam._accuracy_note: Close on hunger and enemies. Disease is not mentioned, and the verse calls for gratitude to God.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I will grant your rains in their season, so that the earth shall yield its produce and the trees of the field their fruit ... you shall eat your fill of bread and dwell securely in your land. I will grant peace in the land ... and no sword shall cross your land.”
judaism.explanation: God promises Israel that if they keep the covenant, their land will have rain, full harvests, security and peace from invasion.
judaism.tie_back: ‘Eat your fill’ and ‘no sword shall cross your land’ are the Torah’s version of a land free from hunger and enemies.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close on famine and enemies; disease is covered later in the chapter’s curses rather than here.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The commentarial tradition says the Ratana Sutta was first taught when the city of Vesali was struck by drought and famine, then by disease, then by harmful spirits drawn by the dead. The Buddha came, the sutta was recited around the city, and the three dangers passed.
buddhism.explanation: The Ratana Sutta is still chanted as a protection because of this story of a city freed from famine, plague and fear.
buddhism.tie_back: Vesali’s three afflictions closely mirror the Kural’s triad of hunger, disease and hostile forces.
buddhism.source: Sutta Nipata 2.1, Ratana Sutta, with its commentary (Piyadassi’s introduction)
buddhism._accuracy_note: A striking parallel triad. The third danger is non-human beings rather than human enemies, and the story comes from the commentary, not the sutta itself.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Peace, the nurse of children, is abroad in their land, and all-seeing Zeus never decrees cruel war against them. Neither famine nor disaster ever haunt men who do true justice.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod describes the city whose people judge fairly: it is spared war, famine and disaster, and the earth feeds it richly.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hesiod’s just city is free of war, famine and disaster, which is almost the Kural’s list of hunger, disease and enemies.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 225-230 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Very close. Hesiod makes the blessing depend on justice, a link the Kural keeps for the chapter’s last verse.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Kautilya devotes a chapter to ‘remedies against national calamities’, naming fire, floods, pestilence, famine, rats, wild beasts, snakes and demons, and prescribing what the state must do against each.
philosophy.explanation: For Kautilya, protecting the land from these disasters is a basic duty of government.
philosophy.tie_back: Kautilya’s list includes the Kural’s famine and pestilence, and treats their absence as a matter of good statecraft.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Shares the concern with famine and disease; hostile armies are dealt with elsewhere in the Arthashastra.

kurals.tamil:
பல்குழுவும் பாழ்செய்யும் உட்பகையும் வேந்தலைக்கும்
கொல்குறும்பும் இல்லது நாடு.
kurals.transliteration:
Palkuzhuvum paazhseyyum utpakaiyum vendhalaikkum
kolkurumpum illadhu naadu.
kurals.meaning: A true country is free of rival factions, of enemies within who bring ruin, and of murderous gangs that trouble the ruler.
kurals.elementary: A sports team can have the best players, but if they split into little groups that fight each other, and some even help the other side, they will lose. A country is the same: it needs its people to pull together.
kurals.university: Where kural 734 dealt with dangers from outside, this one turns to dangers from within. Palkuzhu is ‘many groups’, which Parimelazhagar reads as factions that quarrel among themselves, paazhseyyum utpakai is ‘internal enmity that works ruin’, and vendhalaikkum kolkurumpu is ‘murderous petty chiefs (or bands) that harass the king’; kurumpu can mean a small hill-chief or a gang of marauders. Solomon Pappaiah modernises the list as caste, religious and political factions, disloyal party members, and local strongmen. The theme is developed fully in chapter 89 (Utpakai, Internal Enmity). The ytamizh text prints the last word as ‘இல்லத’, which appears to be a typographical slip for the standard ‘இல்லது’ found in the sandhi text and other editions.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Protect thyself, O king, from all fears that arise from within. Fears, however, that arise from outside are of little consequence. The first kind of fear, O king, may cut thy roots in a single day.”
hinduism.explanation: Bhishma tells Yudhishthira that quarrels and disunion inside a kingdom are far more dangerous than foreign enemies.
hinduism.tie_back: Bhishma and Valluvar agree that internal enmity is the danger that can destroy a land from its roots.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Section 107 (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Direct parallel on the peril of internal enmity and faction, in a passage about the same kind of groups (gana) the Kural calls kuzhu.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Every kingdom divided against itself is brought to desolation; and every city or house divided against itself shall not stand.”
christianity.explanation: Answering critics, Jesus points out that any kingdom torn by internal division will fall.
christianity.tie_back: ‘Brought to desolation’ is close to the Kural’s paazhseyyum, ‘working ruin’: division inside a land destroys it.
christianity._accuracy_note: Very close on the destructiveness of internal division. Jesus uses it as an argument, not as advice on statecraft.

islam.quote_or_event: “And obey Allah and His Messenger, and do not dispute and [thus] lose courage and [then] your strength would depart; and be patient. Indeed, Allah is with the patient.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an warns the believers that quarrelling among themselves will drain away their courage and strength.
islam.tie_back: The strength that ‘departs’ through dispute is what the Kural’s land keeps by being free of factions.
islam._accuracy_note: Good match on the danger of internal dispute. The verse is addressed to a community at war rather than to a settled land.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud asks why the Second Temple was destroyed when the people of that time studied Torah, kept the commandments and did acts of kindness. It answers that there was baseless hatred among them, and teaches that baseless hatred weighs as much as idolatry, forbidden relations and bloodshed together.
judaism.explanation: The rabbis locate the fall of Jerusalem in hatred among Jews themselves, not only in the Roman armies.
judaism.tie_back: Yoma’s teaching is a historical example of the Kural’s ‘internal enmity that works ruin’.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong parallel on internal hatred bringing ruin; the Talmud frames it as a sin before God as well as a political failure.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “What have you heard, Ananda: do the Vajjis assemble and disperse peacefully and attend to their affairs in concord?” ... “So long, Ananda, as this is the case, the growth of the Vajjis is to be expected, not their decline.”
buddhism.explanation: When King Ajatasattu plans to attack the Vajjis, the Buddha says they cannot be defeated as long as they meet often and act in harmony.
buddhism.tie_back: The Buddha’s point is the Kural’s: a people without factions cannot easily be destroyed.
buddhism.source: Digha Nikaya 16, Mahaparinibbana Sutta 1.4 (trans. Sister Vajira and Francis Story)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close fit. The sutta states the positive condition (concord) that the Kural states negatively (no factions).

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At the end of the Oresteia, Athena calls on the Furies, now called the Kindly Ones, to bless Athens, and the chorus prays that civil strife (stasis) may never roar in the city and that citizens may never shed each other’s blood in revenge.
greek_mythology.explanation: The trilogy ends by turning the spirits of vengeance into guardians against civil war.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The prayer against stasis is the Greek form of the Kural’s wish for a land free of faction and murderous internal enemies.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Clear thematic parallel; it is a prayer in drama rather than a definition of a good country.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For indeed any city, however small, is in fact divided into two, one the city of the poor, the other of the rich; these are at war with one another; and in either there are many smaller divisions.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates says most cities are not truly one city but many hostile factions, which is why they are weak.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato’s ‘many cities’ within one city is exactly the Kural’s palkuzhu, the many factions a real land must be free of.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close on factions as the sickness of a state, though Plato traces faction mainly to the gap between rich and poor.

kurals.tamil:
கேடறியாக் கெட்ட இடத்தும் வளங்குன்றா
நாடென்ப நாட்டின் தலை.
kurals.transliteration:
Kedariyaak ketta idaththum valangundraa
naadenpa naattin thalai.
kurals.meaning: The wise say the best of all countries is one that does not know ruin, and even when harm does come, does not lose its richness.
kurals.elementary: A strong tree is rarely hurt by storms, and even when a branch breaks, it keeps giving fruit. The best country is like that tree: hardly ever harmed, and quick to stay fruitful even when it is.
kurals.university: The kural has two degrees of excellence: kedariyaa (‘not knowing ruin’) and, failing that, ketta idaththum valam kundraa (‘even when ruined, its richness does not decline’). Parimelazhagar takes the ruin to be damage from enemies, and Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah follow him, while Kalaignar reads it as any kind of harm that the land’s resources are great enough to repair. Enpa (‘they say’) marks the judgment as the view of the learned, and naattin thalai means ‘the head, or foremost, of lands’. The idea is resilience: the best land is judged not only by its good years but by how it comes through bad ones. The ytamizh text reads ‘நாட்டின் தலை’ and the sandhi text ‘நாட்டிற் தலை’, a difference of joining only.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Puranic story of King Prithu, the earth withholds her crops during a time of disorder and famine. Prithu pursues the earth, who has taken the form of a cow, and she agrees to yield again; he levels the land, and the earth is ‘milked’ so that grain and plenty return.
hinduism.explanation: The earth is named Prithvi after him, because he restored her fruitfulness after it had failed.
hinduism.tie_back: Prithu’s earth recovers its abundance after ruin, the second and harder test of the Kural’s best land.
hinduism.source: Vishnu Purana 1.13 and Bhagavata Purana 4.18 (story of Prithu)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Matches the theme of fruitfulness restored after disaster, but credits a king rather than the land’s own resilience.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat upon that house; and it fell not: for it was founded upon a rock.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus compares those who live by his words to a man who built his house on rock, which survived the storm.
christianity.tie_back: The house that is struck but ‘fell not’ is a picture of the Kural’s land that stays whole even when ruin comes.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shares the image of withstanding disaster, but it is a parable about personal faith, not about a country.

islam.quote_or_event: “Then will come after that seven difficult [years] which will consume what you saved for them, except a little from which you will store.”
islam.explanation: Joseph interprets the king’s dream and tells Egypt to store the surplus of seven good years, so that the land can survive seven years of famine.
islam.tie_back: Joseph’s Egypt is the Kural’s best land: when disaster strikes, its stores keep its richness from failing.
islam._accuracy_note: Good match on resilience through reserves. The Qur’an’s focus is Joseph’s wisdom rather than the land.

judaism.quote_or_event: Genesis tells that when famine struck the land, Isaac stayed in Gerar at God’s word, sowed there, and reaped a hundredfold in that same year, and grew very wealthy.
judaism.explanation: Even in a year of famine, Isaac’s fields flourished.
judaism.tie_back: Isaac’s hundredfold harvest in a famine year is an image of a land whose richness does not fail even in bad times.
judaism._accuracy_note: Captures abundance in a time of ruin, but the blessing belongs to one man, not to a whole country.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Truly, Ananda, as far as the Aryan race extends and trade routes spread, this will be the foremost city Pataliputta, a trade-center. But Pataliputta, Ananda, will be assailed by three perils — fire, water, and dissension.”
buddhism.explanation: Seeing the fort being built at Pataligama, the Buddha predicts it will become the greatest city of the region, but also names the dangers it will face.
buddhism.tie_back: The Buddha, like Valluvar, speaks of a ‘foremost’ land and knows that even the best land will meet danger.
buddhism.source: Digha Nikaya 16, Mahaparinibbana Sutta 1.28 (trans. Sister Vajira and Francis Story)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Shares the idea of the foremost city exposed to ruin, but says nothing about keeping its wealth after harm.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Homeric Hymn to Demeter, the grieving goddess makes the earth barren for a year, and famine threatens all mankind. When her daughter Persephone is returned, Demeter lets the fields grow again, and the whole earth is heavy with leaves and flowers.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth explains how the land can be struck barren and then return to full growth.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Demeter’s earth, ruined and then made fruitful again, reflects the Kural’s land whose richness comes back even after harm.
greek_mythology.source: Homeric Hymn to Demeter (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good image of recovery. In the myth the earth is barren for a time, whereas the Kural’s best land does not lose its richness at all.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Machiavelli argues that a prince whose city is well fortified, stocked with a year’s food, drink and fuel, and whose people are kept at work, cannot easily be taken, because an enemy cannot keep a siege going that long.
philosophy.explanation: For Machiavelli, a city’s strength lies in its reserves as much as in its walls.
philosophy.tie_back: Machiavelli’s well-stocked city is the Kural’s best land: even when it is attacked, its wealth does not fail.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong on resilience under attack; Machiavelli writes about a single fortified city rather than a whole country.

kurals.tamil:
இருபுனலும் வாய்ந்த மலையும் வருபுனலும்
வல்லரணும் நாட்டிற்கு உறுப்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
Irupunalum vaaindha malaiyum varupunalum
vallaranum naattirku uruppu.
kurals.meaning: The limbs of a country are its two kinds of water, well-placed hills, the water that flows down from them, and a strong fortress.
kurals.elementary: A castle in a story often sits by a river, with hills behind it, springs nearby and high walls around it. Water keeps people alive, and hills and walls keep them safe. Valluvar says a country needs all of these, like a body needs arms and legs.
kurals.university: Uruppu means ‘limb’ or ‘organ’, so the kural presents the natural features of a land as parts of a living body. Parimelazhagar reads irupunal (‘the two waters’) as water from below (springs, wells) and water from above (rain), and varupunal (‘the water that comes’) as rivers flowing from the hills; the hills themselves are vaaindha (well situated) because they feed the rivers and shelter the land. Kalaignar instead reads irupunal as river and sea, and varupunal as rain. Vallaran, the ‘strong fortress’, anticipates the next chapter, Aran, where hills, water and forest reappear as natural defences. The sandhi text reads ‘வல்லரணு நாட்டிற் குறுப்பு’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Let him build (there) a town, making for his safety a fortress, protected by a desert, or a fortress built of (stone and) earth, or one protected by water or trees, or one (formed by an encampment of armed) men or a hill-fort. Let him make every effort to secure a hill-fort, for amongst all those (fortresses mentioned) a hill-fort is distinguished by many superior qualities.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu lists the kinds of fortress a king may build, protected by desert, earth, water, forest, men or hills, and says the hill-fort is best.
hinduism.tie_back: Manu’s water, hill and forest forts are the same natural defences the Kural names as limbs of a country.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close on hills and water as defences; Manu is concerned with the fort alone, while the Kural also values water for life.

christianity.quote_or_event: “There is a river, the streams whereof shall make glad the city of God, the holy place of the tabernacles of the most High. God is in the midst of her; she shall not be moved.”
christianity.explanation: The psalmist sings of Jerusalem as a city refreshed by a river and made unshakable by God’s presence.
christianity.tie_back: A river that gives life and a city that ‘shall not be moved’ match the Kural’s pairing of water and strong defence.
christianity._accuracy_note: Water and security are both present, but the psalm’s river and defence are largely spiritual.

islam.quote_or_event: “And He has cast into the earth firmly set mountains, lest it shift with you, and [made] rivers and roads, that you may be guided.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an names mountains and rivers among the signs of God’s care for people on earth.
islam.tie_back: Mountains and rivers are two of the Kural’s limbs of a land, here presented as God’s gifts.
islam._accuracy_note: Same features (mountains and rivers), but cited as signs of God rather than as parts of a well-ordered country.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Psalms say that as the mountains surround Jerusalem, so the LORD surrounds his people from now and for ever.
judaism.explanation: The hills around Jerusalem are used as a picture of God’s protection.
judaism.tie_back: The psalm takes for granted what the Kural says outright: surrounding hills are a land’s natural defence.
judaism._accuracy_note: Matches the idea of hills as protection; water and fortress are not mentioned.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There is the case where the royal frontier fortress has large stores of grass, timber & water for the delight, convenience, & comfort of those within, and to ward off those without.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes a royal frontier fortress with a deep moat, high ramparts and stores of water and food, which cannot be taken by enemies. He uses it as a picture of a well-guarded mind.
buddhism.tie_back: The fortress needs water and strong walls together, as the Kural’s country needs its waters and its vallaran.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 7.63, Nagara Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close on water supply and fortification as the basis of security. The sutta uses them as a metaphor for spiritual practice.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “It is rugged and not a good driving country, but it is by no means a bad island for what there is of it. It grows any quantity of corn and also wine, for it is watered both by rain and dew ... and there are watering places where the water never runs dry.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Athena, in disguise, describes Ithaca to the returning Odysseus: rocky and hilly, but watered by rain and by springs that never fail.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Rain from above and springs that never run dry are exactly Parimelazhagar’s ‘two waters’, set in a hilly land.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Striking match on the two kinds of water and the hills; there is no fortress in the passage.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “It should afford easy egress to the citizens, and at the same time be inaccessible and difficult of capture to enemies. There should be a natural abundance of springs and fountains in the town, or, if there is a deficiency of them, great reservoirs may be established for the collection of rainwater.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle sets out the ideal site for a city: hard for enemies to reach, with plentiful springs, or cisterns for rainwater.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle, like Valluvar, names spring water, rain water and natural defence as essentials of a good territory.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Remarkably close, down to the two sources of water; Aristotle adds health and air.

kurals.tamil:
பிணியின்மை செல்வம் விளைவின்பம் ஏமம்
அணியென்ப நாட்டிற்கிவ் வைந்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Piniyinmai selvam vilaivinpam emam
aniyenpa naattirkiv vaindhu.
kurals.meaning: The learned say a country has five ornaments: freedom from disease, wealth, good harvests, happiness and security.
kurals.elementary: A birthday cake looks best with candles, icing, fruit, sprinkles and a name on top. A country has its own five decorations: healthy people, enough money, good crops, happy faces and safe streets.
kurals.university: Ani means ‘ornament’ or ‘jewel’, so where kural 737 listed the land’s limbs (uruppu), this one lists its adornments. The five are piniyinmai (absence of disease), selvam (wealth), vilaivu (produce), inpam (enjoyment, happiness) and emam (safety, protection); Parimelazhagar glosses emam as the protection given to subjects. Mu. Varadarasanar and Pope follow the same five, while some modern readers join vilaivu and inpam as ‘the joy of harvest’. The verse sums up the chapter’s positive ideal in a single list. The ytamizh text prints the second line as ‘அணியென்ப நாட்டிவ் வைந்து’, but the sandhi text and the standard editions read ‘நாட்டிற்கிவ் வைந்து’ (naattirku + iv + aindhu, ‘these five for a land’), which is needed for the metre and is followed here.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “In consequence again of royal protection, men can everywhere sleep fearlessly and at their case without shutting their houses and doors with bolts and bars.”
hinduism.explanation: Brihaspati tells King Vasumanas that good royal protection lets people live without fear, so that they can sleep with their doors unlocked.
hinduism.tie_back: Sleeping with open doors is a vivid picture of emam, the security that is one of the Kural’s five ornaments of a land.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Section 68 (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong on security. It covers only one of the five ornaments, and ‘case’ is a typo for ‘ease’ in the online Ganguli text.

christianity.quote_or_event: “That our garners may be full, affording all manner of store: that our sheep may bring forth thousands and ten thousands in our streets: That our oxen may be strong to labour; that there be no breaking in, nor going out; that there be no complaining in our streets. Happy is that people, that is in such a case.”
christianity.explanation: The psalmist prays for full barns, growing flocks, strong oxen, no invasion and no distress, and calls such a people happy.
christianity.tie_back: Full barns, no breaking in and a happy people are the Kural’s produce, security and joy in one prayer.
christianity._accuracy_note: Very close list of a land’s blessings; health is not named directly.

islam.quote_or_event: “And [mention] when Abraham said, ‘My Lord, make this a secure city and provide its people with fruits.’”
islam.explanation: Abraham prays for Mecca to be a safe city whose people are fed with fruit.
islam.tie_back: Abraham asks for two of the Kural’s ornaments, security and produce, as the essentials of a good city.
islam._accuracy_note: Matches security and harvest; health, wealth and joy are not mentioned.

judaism.quote_or_event: “But they shall sit every man under his vine and under his fig-tree; And none shall make them afraid.”
judaism.explanation: Micah pictures a time of peace when everyone enjoys the fruit of his own land without fear.
judaism.tie_back: Sitting under one’s own vine without fear joins produce, happiness and security, three of the Kural’s five ornaments.
judaism._accuracy_note: A classic image of the ideal land; health and wealth are implied rather than stated.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Health is the most precious gain and contentment the greatest wealth. A trustworthy person is the best kinsman, Nibbana the highest bliss.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada ranks health first among gains and contentment as the truest wealth.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural also puts freedom from disease first among a land’s ornaments, followed by wealth and happiness.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Shares health, wealth and happiness as goods, but speaks of the individual, not the country.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod tells that Zeus married Themis, who bore the Horai: Eunomia (Good Order), Dike (Justice) and Eirene (Peace), goddesses who watch over the works of mortal men.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Greek myth, order, justice and peace are divine sisters who make human communities flourish.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Horai are, in effect, the ornaments of a well-ordered land, as the Kural’s five are.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Parallel in listing the goods that adorn a society, but the Horai are moral and civic qualities, not material ones.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “We may define happiness as prosperity combined with virtue; or as independence of life; or as the secure enjoyment of the maximum of pleasure; or as a good condition of property and body, together with the power of guarding one's property and body and making use of them.”
philosophy.explanation: In his guide for political speakers, Aristotle sets out the commonly agreed parts of happiness, including wealth, health and the secure enjoyment of life, and applies several of them to whole communities as well as to individuals.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle's list of what makes life good overlaps closely with the Kural's ornaments of a country, which are health, wealth, happiness and security.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Rhetoric, I.5, 1360b (tr. W. Rhys Roberts)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on the MIT Internet Classics Archive (Rhys Roberts). Partial match: Aristotle's list is mainly of an individual's happiness, and harvests are absent, but health, prosperity, enjoyment and security all appear, and the chapter applies some of them to states.

kurals.tamil:
நாடென்ப நாடா வளத்தன நாடல்ல
நாட வளந்தரு நாடு.
kurals.transliteration:
Naadenpa naadaa valaththana naadalla
naada valandharu naadu.
kurals.meaning: The learned call those lands true countries whose wealth comes without being sought; a land that gives wealth only when laboriously sought is not a true country.
kurals.elementary: Some gardens grow fruit almost by themselves because the soil and rain are just right. Other gardens need you to dig, water and fight weeds every day for a tiny crop. Valluvar says the best country is like the first garden.
kurals.university: The kural is built on a pun between naadu (‘country’) and the verb naadu (‘to seek, to search for’): naadaa valaththana are lands ‘whose wealth is not sought’, and naada valandharu naadu is a land ‘that gives wealth only when sought’. Parimelazhagar explains that the best lands produce their riches by natural endowment, without great exertion by the inhabitants, while lands that yield only to heavy labour are not counted as countries in the full sense. The line is not a praise of idleness, since the Kural elsewhere (chapter 62, Aalvinaiyudaimai) insists on effort; it is a judgment on natural endowment. Kalaignar makes this explicit by contrasting lands naturally rich with lands that prosper only through constant struggle.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Mahabharata’s description of the Uttarakurus, the northern land of the blessed, tells of trees that bear fruit and flowers in every season and yield whatever the people need, so that they live in ease without labouring for their food.
hinduism.explanation: Uttarakuru is the Indian image of a land that gives everything by nature.
hinduism.tie_back: Uttarakuru is the extreme case of the Kural’s ideal: a land whose wealth comes without being sought.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Bhishma Parva, Jambu-khanda section (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Good image of effortless abundance, but it is a mythical paradise rather than a real country.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For the earth bringeth forth fruit of herself; first the blade, then the ear, after that the full corn in the ear.”
christianity.explanation: In a parable of the kingdom of God, Jesus describes seed growing by itself while the farmer sleeps, without his knowing how.
christianity.tie_back: ‘Fruit of herself’ is close to the Kural’s naadaa valam, wealth that grows without being laboriously sought.
christianity._accuracy_note: Nice verbal echo; the parable is about the growth of God’s kingdom, not about the richness of a land.

islam.quote_or_event: “And Allāh presents an example: a city [i.e., Makkah] which was safe and secure, its provision coming to it in abundance from every location, but it denied the favors of Allāh. So Allāh made it taste the envelopment of hunger and fear for what they had been doing.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes a city whose provision came to it plentifully from everywhere, until its ingratitude brought hunger and fear.
islam.tie_back: Provision ‘coming to it’ from every side is the Kural’s land whose wealth arrives without being sought.
islam._accuracy_note: Close on wealth that comes of itself; the verse’s main point is the loss of it through ingratitude.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For the land, whither thou goest in to possess it, is not as the land of Egypt, from whence ye came out, where thou didst sow thy seed, and didst water it with thy foot, as a garden of herbs; but the land, whither ye go over to possess it, is a land of hills and valleys, and drinketh water as the rain of heaven cometh down.”
judaism.explanation: Moses contrasts Egypt, where fields must be watered by hard irrigation work, with the promised land, which is watered by rain from heaven.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s very contrast: a land that yields only through toil versus a land that yields by its own nature.
judaism._accuracy_note: Nearly the same comparison; Deuteronomy adds that the rain depends on God’s care and Israel’s faithfulness.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Agganna Sutta the Buddha tells how, at the beginning of the world, rice grew by itself, clean and ready to eat, and whatever was gathered in the evening grew back by morning. Only when beings began to hoard it did the self-growing rice disappear, so that they had to plough, sow and divide the fields.
buddhism.explanation: The sutta explains the origin of labour, property and kingship as a fall from a time of effortless plenty.
buddhism.tie_back: The self-growing rice is the Buddhist picture of wealth that comes without being sought, the Kural’s ideal.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close image of unsought abundance; the sutta places it in a lost golden age and treats its loss as a moral lesson.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “For the fruitful earth unforced bare them fruit abundantly and without stint. They dwelt in ease and peace upon their lands with many good things.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod describes the golden race of men under Cronos, who lived without toil because the earth fed them of its own accord.
greek_mythology.tie_back: ‘The earth unforced’ is almost a translation of the Kural’s naadaa valam, wealth that is not sought.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 116-119 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Very close on unsought abundance, though Hesiod describes a vanished age rather than a present country.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Statesman, Plato’s Stranger tells the myth of the age of Cronus, when people had fruit in plenty from trees and plants that the earth gave of its own accord, without farming, and needed no political constitutions.
philosophy.explanation: Plato uses the myth to contrast a divinely cared-for age of plenty with the present age, in which people must work and govern themselves.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato’s myth gives a philosophical frame to the Kural’s contrast between lands rich by nature and lands rich only through toil.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Parallel image; Plato questions whether such ease makes people happy, which the Kural does not ask.

kurals.tamil:
ஆங்கமை வெய்தியக் கண்ணும் பயமின்றே
வேந்தமை வில்லாத நாடு.
kurals.transliteration:
Aangamai veydhiyak kannum payamindre
vendhamai villaadha naadu.
kurals.meaning: Even if a land has every good quality described above, it is of no use if it lacks a fitting ruler in harmony with it.
kurals.elementary: You can have the best football, the greenest field and the fastest players, but without a good captain who works well with the team, you will not win. A country with every treasure still needs a good leader.
kurals.university: The chapter ends by subordinating everything it has praised to kingship. Aangu amaivu eydhiya kannum means ‘even when it has attained all the excellences set out there’ (in the previous nine kurals), and payam indre means ‘it is without fruit’. The key compound vendhamaivu is read by Parimelazhagar as ‘harmony, or fitness, between king and subjects’, which Pope follows with ‘not with its king at peace’; Mu. Varadarasanar, Kalaignar and Sivayogi Sivakumar read it more simply as ‘a good king or good government’, and Solomon Pappaiah as a government with love for its citizens. Either way, the verse links this chapter back to the Kural’s section on kingship (Arasiyal) and warns that natural wealth without right rule is wasted. The sandhi text agrees with ytamizh word for word.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The world depends upon agriculture and trade and is protected by the Vedas. All these again are duly protected by the king exercising his principal duty.”
hinduism.explanation: Brihaspati tells King Vasumanas that without royal protection, farming and trade would collapse, the strong would rob the weak and famine would ravage the kingdom.
hinduism.tie_back: Brihaspati makes the Kural’s point: all a land’s wealth depends on a king who fulfils his duty.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Section 68 (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close; the Mahabharata stresses fear of anarchy, while Parimelazhagar’s reading stresses harmony between ruler and people.

christianity.quote_or_event: “The king by judgment establisheth the land: but he that receiveth gifts overthroweth it.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb says a just king makes a country stable, while a corrupt one brings it down.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, the proverb makes the fate of the land depend on the quality of its ruler.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close in spirit; Proverbs stresses justice and bribery, the Kural harmony between king and land.

islam.quote_or_event: “Surely! Everyone of you is a guardian and is responsible for his charges: The Imam (ruler) of the people is a guardian and is responsible for his subjects.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that every person, and above all the ruler, is a guardian answerable for those in his care.
islam.tie_back: The ruler as guardian of his people is the bond (vendhamaivu) without which, the Kural says, a rich land is useless.
islam._accuracy_note: Matches the ruler’s responsibility for his people; it does not say that a land’s wealth is worthless without him.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi Hanina, the vice-high priest said: pray for the welfare of the government, for were it not for the fear it inspires, every man would swallow his neighbor alive.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah teaches that even an imperfect government is a blessing, because without it society would fall into violence.
judaism.tie_back: Rabbi Hanina, like Valluvar, holds that a land without working rule gains nothing from its other goods.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close on the necessity of government; the Mishnah speaks of order, the Kural of harmony between king and land.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha teaches that when kings are unrighteous, their officials and then the whole people become unrighteous; the sun and moon go astray, the rains fail to come in season, the crops ripen badly, and people become weak and short-lived. When kings are righteous, the reverse happens.
buddhism.explanation: In this teaching, the moral quality of the ruler flows down through the people into nature itself.
buddhism.tie_back: The Buddha’s point is the Kural’s: a land’s fertility and well-being are worthless, even lost, without a righteous ruler.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close on the ruler’s effect on the land; the sutta makes the link cosmic, while the Kural keeps it practical.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “You are like some blameless king, who upholds righteousness, as the monarch over a great and valiant nation: the earth yields its wheat and barley, the trees are loaded with fruit, the ewes bring forth lambs, and the sea abounds with fish by reason of his virtues.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus, in disguise, praises Penelope by comparing her to a just king whose goodness makes the whole land fruitful.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Homer, like Valluvar, makes the land’s abundance depend on the quality of its king.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Very close; Homer states the positive case (good king, fruitful land), the Kural the negative.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Republic, Socrates says that cities will never have rest from their evils until philosophers become kings, or kings and rulers become true philosophers, so that political power and wisdom meet in one person.
philosophy.explanation: For Plato, the right ruler is the one condition without which no city can be good.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato and Valluvar both end their picture of the good city by insisting that everything depends on the right kind of ruler.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Same structure of argument; Plato demands wisdom in the ruler, the Kural harmony between ruler and land.
